To the Reader, greetings.

You are to be advised, candid reader, that of the letters R. and S. in this work, placed sometimes over numbers, sometimes over characters, sometimes over words, either superscribed on the page or added in the margin, the former is the mark of rubric, or red color, while the latter is the mark of ink, or black color. Moreover you will observe this too: the individual titles of the individual chapters are likewise to be depicted and adorned in rubric. You may seek the significance of this matter from the Key prefixed to the work. Farewell.

Here begins the first book of the Steganographia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, addressed to the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and prince elector of the Holy Empire, etc.

It is the opinion of the most learned that the most ancient sages, whom in Greek speech we call philosophers, if they had discovered any secrets either of nature or of art, concealed them by various modes and figures, lest they come to the knowledge of wicked men. That Moses too, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of Heaven and Earth covered over the ineffable secrets of mysteries with simple words, all the more learned among the Jews confirm. Saint Jerome also, most learned among our own, affirms that almost as many mysteries lie hidden in the Apocalypse of John as there are words. Besides, I pass over the sages of the Greeks, held in no small esteem among their own people, and our own most learned philosophers and poets, who, devoting their effort to writing fables, [unclear] one thing to the unlearned, and another to learned men
Preface.

They handed them down, in a sequence of narration, by sagacious invention. Although, because of the dullness of my talent, I cannot perfectly imitate these most devoted lovers of wisdom, nevertheless I do not cease to admire them and to read them with whatever diligence I can. For when I consider that they, by their own study, devised great things beyond other men, I rub myself, as it were, with a certain force, so that I may grow warm, and I impel myself toward some imitation, even among the least, of those who have gone before.

Nor, as I think, has this opinion wholly deceived me; since through the continual pursuit of reading I have learned many things which I had not known before, and it has opened to my thoughts an approach to investigating matters more secret and altogether hidden from others. For although I am not of such learning or industry that I would dare profess that I have in every respect grasped the hidden method of the mysteries of the ancient sages, nevertheless I have found certain methods, many and various, not altogether contemptible, as it seems to me, by which I can safely and without deception, suspicion, or detection by anyone, through open messengers or letters, convey to another the most secret intention of my mind in this art of knowledge as widely as I may wish.

And at the request of the Most Serene Prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, always my most unwilling [unclear], the wisest Maecenas of all philosophers, than whom no one has seemed to me more worthy for this great secret to be revealed to him, I have committed to writing this new discovery of a most secret art, and not without the greatest labors have gathered it into the present volume. But lest this great secret come to the ears of common, unskilled, or wicked men, the reckoning of my office judged it not least important so to wrap it, since it teaches one ignorant of mysteries to understand them, in mysteries, that there will be no one from the number of the unskilled, no one except the most studious, who can by his own power perfectly penetrate the secret of this knowledge, and fully according to our intention, unless by reception from a teacher,
Preface.

... the letters of the world, Latin, Greek, or barbarous, free from all suspicion, by which it would present one thing openly to those ignorant of the art, and another secretly to those who knew it. Nor, if this science were published among the reprobate, would the trust between married persons, contracted by sacrament, any longer remain safe thereafter: since a wife, even if hitherto ignorant of the Latin tongue, yet now sufficiently instructed, through modest, honorable, and most holy words of any language or idiom, could understand most fully the evil and immodest mind and intention of an adulterous lover or fornicator, even while her husband carried the letters and praised them as excellent; and she could, in the same way, as broadly and copiously as she wished, most safely communicate her own desire to him in the same or other letters, in a beautiful and quite highly adorned sequence. And public trust could be endangered; all letters, documents, writings, and finally the very knowledge of men could come [unclear] (which God forbid); the whole order of the commonwealth, with the passage of time, could be disturbed in no small degree.

Nor can anyone, even if he lived as many years, ever become so learned and experienced in this science with his teacher that there would not be left infinite methods, secretly, most hiddenly, and most safely sufficient in this very art of writing, and, at the will of any experienced person, of working for all purposes, which he himself has not yet grasped with his preceptor. For just as the aerial spirits, good and evil, created by the highest God for our ministry and benefit, through whose understanding all the secrets of this art are revealed, are countless, infinite, and utterly incomprehensible to us, so too [unclear] of this art of ours, which [is called] secret Steganography...
Preface.

[un]covered secrets and hidden things and mysteries, perfectly containing things open to no mortal, however studious or learned, we call [unclear]; all the modes, ways, differences, qualities, and operations will be able to be made fully penetrable forever. For this science is a chaos of infinite depth, which no one can perfectly comprehend, because however learned and experienced you may be in this art, nevertheless you have always grasped less than that which you do not know. For this profound and most secret art has this property: that it easily renders the pupil incomparably, so to speak, more learned than the master, provided he is disposed by nature to proceed, and is studious in those things which he has received in the Cabalistic tradition.
The author's protestation or oath concerning the innocence of this art, etc.

And lest any future reader of this work, when in the course of it he has often encountered names, offices, orders, differences, properties, prayers, and any other operations of spirits, through whose intelligences all these secrets of this science are closed and opened, should believe or think me a necromancer and magician, or that I have entered into a pact with demons, or that I have used, or use, any other superstition: I have considered it necessary and opportune, by vindicating it with truth, to preserve my reputation and name from so great a stain, injury, fault, and blemish by a solemn protestation in this prologue.

Therefore I say before Almighty God, from whom absolutely nothing can be hidden, and before Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, who will judge the living and the dead; in truth I say, swear, and protest: all and every one of the things which I have said in this work, or am about to say, and all the properties, modes, figures, operations, receptions, formations, inventions, institutions, mutations, alterations of this science or art, and all things whatsoever which pertain to its speculation, invention, attainment, practical operation, either in part or in whole, and everything contained in this volume of ours, rest upon true, Catholic, natural principles; and all and every one of them are done with God, with a good conscience, without injury to the Christian faith, with the integrity of ecclesiastical tradition, without any superstition, without idolatry, without any explicit or implicit pact with evil spirits; without suffumigation, adoration, veneration, worship, sacrifice, or offering to demons; without any fault or sin, whether venial or mortal. And all and every one of them are done with truth, uprightness, sincerity, and purity. So that the science of this invention, besides, for good use,
Preface.

[unclear] use, nothing that would not befit a wise man, a good and faithful Christian. For I too am a Christian, and voluntarily devoted to the monastic way of life; and I desire to live and conduct myself in no other way than befits a true Christian and a monk professed under the Rule of the blessed father Benedict. I received the Catholic faith itself, according to the tradition of the holy Roman Church, from the cradle, baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. This faith I hold and believe together with that same universal Church of Christians; and, as long as I live, with God’s help always firmly preserving it inviolate, I shall hold it in heart, mouth, and deed, nor do I ever intend to deviate from it on any occasion whatever. Far be it from me, therefore, either to learn or to teach anything contrary to the Christian faith and its purity, harmful to holy morals, or in any way opposed to the regular profession. I fear God, and I have sworn myself to his worship; from him I shall not be separated while living, nor, as I trust, when dead.

I have placed this declaration of mine at the head of this whole work of ours not without cause, because I know that there will be many who, when they cannot understand what we have written, will turn to insults and will attribute our good and holy studies to evil arts or superstitious admonitions. To these, since they will exist, and to all who are going to read these synthemata of ours, we earnestly entreat that, if they understand this secret tradition of ours, they keep it forever hidden, and not pour such wondrous mysteries out into public. But if they do not understand it, as we know will happen to many, let them learn before they criticize. For indeed he shows himself a rash judge who, before he has known the truth of a case, pronounces sentence upon it. Learn this art first, and judge afterward; but if you cannot understand it, reject not the art itself, since it is good, but your own dull wits. For I know and am certain that no one of holy mind can criticize this work of ours unless he happens to be wholly ignorant of it. But those for whom it is more familiar to despise wisdom than to have learned it, I neither desire nor would wish to penetrate these mysteries of ours.
Chapter.
Chapter I.

Whose key and operation are held by the principal spirit Pamersyel, anoyr madriel, through the ministry of ebra sothean abrulges utrasbiel. And nadres ormenu i tules rablion hamorphiel. To these the commission of all is made with an exorcism.
[unclear]

The operation of this first chapter is very difficult and full of dangers, because of the pride and rebellion of its spirits, who do not obey anyone unless he is most experienced in this art. For they not only do not obey novices and those less proved in the art, but also, if they are pressed too much, they frequently harm them and offend them with various illusions. They are malicious and faithless above all other aerial spirits, and obey absolutely no one unless compelled by the greatest sacraments; and the secret entrusted to them they often faithlessly reveal to others. For as soon as they have been sent out with letters, they fly off, and, bursting in without order toward the person to whom they are sent, like a people fleeing from battle without a leader, they hasten furiously and, filling the air with their shouting, often disclose all the secrets around the sender. Therefore we advise that no one intending to operate in this art should compel them, nor anxiously seek their services. For they are insolent and faithless, since he can find many of those whom we shall mention next who are sufficiently well-disposed, and who of their own accord offer themselves ready for obedience. But if anyone should wholly wish to experience their insolence and to prove that what we have said is true, let him know that this manner must be observed. Let him prepare the paper on which he is going to write, with an invocation of the divine name, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Then let him write on it whatever simple and open narrative he wishes

open, which all who read will understand, in Latin, in the native tongue, or in any other language. But when he has sat down to write, facing the East, let him compel the spirits thus: Pamerfiel oshurmy delmuson Thafloyn peano charustea melany, lyaminto colehan, paroys, madyn, moerlay, bulre + atloot don melcoue peloin, ibutsyl meon mysbreath alini driaco person. Crisolnay, lemon asosle mydar, icoriel pean thalmon, asophiel il notreon banyel ocimos esteuor naelma besrona thulaomor fronian beldodrayn bon otalmesgo mero fas elnathyn boframoth. When he has said these things, and has seen that the spirits are present to him for obedience, let him continue the work begun. But if they have not yet appeared, let him repeat the things already said so many times until they appear; or else let him cease altogether, lest, compelled too much, they harm the operator. But when you have completed the letters intended, send them with a messenger to a friend approved in the art; when he receives them, let him say this conjuration: Lamarton anoyr bulon madriel traschon ebrasothea panthenon nabruilges Camery itrasbier rubanthy nadres Calmosy ormenulan, ytules demy rabion hamorphyn. When these things have been said, he will at once understand your meaning perfectly, the spirits now of their own accord offering themselves with force and crying out, so that very often even others present can perceive the sender's secret. But observe that in all letters which you send written by this art you affix your own sign, so that the man to whom you write may know through which spirits you have operated. For if he were to operate through some spirits for understanding, and you through others for sending, they will never obey him for all eternity; rather, because of the improper operation, they would both harm him and by no means reveal your secret. For all the spirits whom we use in this art guard only the ranks and offices committed to them; in no way do they interfere with others. Consider carefully all the things which we shall say in what follows. And, so that we may prove by example the things we have said, let us set out our intention in the vernacular tongue, which we shall subsequently make known to a friend in the aforesaid manner.
Let there be
Book One.
Let this be the secret intention of the mind of Roth, some prince, which he wishes his absent vassal to know.

Dear faithful one, it is our will, for honest cause, to make war on those of Strasbourg and to fall upon them with all our force next Wednesday after Vitus and Modestus. Therefore it is our earnest desire of you, since you are bound to us by oath and vow and obliged to faithful services: that on that same day you should appear well equipped, according to your ability, about four after midday, by Stauffenburg in the forest [Here the letters were placed thus]; you would find further instruction there, should follow it, and should not fail to come. We shall recognize this graciously toward you, and keep this plan of ours with you in high secrecy, etc.
For making this secret known to Roth's vassal, with the fuller intention of the sender, let it be written thus or in another way:
[unclear]

Almighty, everlasting God, who created all things out of nothing, have mercy on us through the most bitter passion of your only-begotten Son dying on the cross, who, conceived of the Holy Spirit without male commingling, was born of the most pure ever-Virgin Mary, and who, giving himself up voluntarily to death for us, by his most holy blood, as he died, freed our souls from death. Hear us wretched ones, O most merciful Father, and through the shedding of the most sacred blood of the same, your sweetest Son Jesus Christ, forgive us our sins and pour your grace into our hearts, so that, loving you in all things and above all things with sincere fervor, we may always obey your commandments with devotion, and, continually advancing in mutual love, henceforth love nothing earthly, seek nothing perishable. For you are the Lord our God, who created us from the beginning in your image and likeness when we did not exist; whom, dead for our sins and buried
Of the Steganography

... buried, you raised from the dead on the third day, and showed him alive for forty days, to the great consolation of his rejoicing disciples. With pure and most firm confession we believe that he, true God and man, reigning with you in your uncircumscribable majesty without end, will come again to judge the living and the dead, and will render to each of us according to his works. Through him we ask you, O most merciful Father: hear us and have mercy on us now and in that terrible hour in which we are to be judged through that Son of yours. Look upon us, most merciful God; for we are frail sinners deserving pity, bare of good works, who by sinning have offended your most holy Majesty in many things. But, turned by your mercy to repentance, we groan weeping for our sins, humbly beseeching through Jesus Christ your Son that you turn your indignation away from us, and mercifully forgive us our past crimes, bringing us, when this present exile is ended, to the delight of the heavenly fatherland. Johannes Trithemius wrote this.

A simple and open narrative of this kind, or any other you wish, which all may read and understand, which contains nothing secret, and which you are not afraid should come before the sight of everyone, you are to write on the aforesaid paper, which we have mentioned, with the conjuration of the spirits, your face turned toward the east. When it has been written, express before the spirits the secret intention that you wish the absent person to know, calling them to witness that they should act faithfully. And at once they will [unclear]. When he to whom your letters are sent has received them, once the sign of the east is known, let him turn his face toward the east and say the conjuration which we have set forth above: Lamarton, a noyr. And at once he will certainly understand your secret intention which you entrusted to the spirits.
Book One. For Knowing the Places, Names, Signs, and Assigned Marks of the Spirits.

But since it is necessary for everyone working in this science to know the places, names, and signs of the principal spirits, lest through ignorance he call from the north one who is dwelling in the south, which would not only hinder his purpose but could also injure the operator, I shall therefore set before you, in a circle, the regions in which the principal spirits dwell, with their names and signs.
Rubric.
In this figure there is an engraver's error: Podiel and Cimuel for Camuel.

Behold, now you have all the regions of the world, which it is necessary above all else to know first in the practice of the art in the present book; without knowledge of them no result will follow in the art.

Further, you must know the first substitutes of each of the princes: how many they are in number, to whom the secret mysteries are entrusted, so that you may know their orders, how they in turn are to be sent forth to their offices, how many illuminators they have in the day, how many luci-
Roth.

light-fleeing ones in the night, and which friends, and how many enemies they are accustomed to fear; and concerning all these things I shall instruct you in the present table, which is called the table of direction.

Here I wish you to understand by east not where the sun rises on any given day, but that place in which it was created at the beginning, which we call the equinoctial. For unless you observe this consideration most diligently, you will not be able to make progress in this art. But now I shall also teach you the [sequence?] of this table, so that from one spirit you may understand all. Let us therefore take Malgaras as an example, through whom the operation of this art is carried out in the ninth chapter of this present first book. He is western; his sign is this: ⋒. He has under him thirty who preside over the day, and they have great command for putting to flight the spirits of darkness. Subject to these are another thirty, who preside over the night and dwell always in darkness; nor do they come to the light except by the command of their princes, to whom they are subject at all times. And these in turn have under them, as guardians and ministers subject to them by full right, sometimes thirty, sometimes twenty, sometimes ten, and sometimes all; they go forth together with all at the command of their principals, and in [unclear] order. Thus, as many of their number as have been summoned by the operator, at the command of the great virtues, from the second or third order, so many servants and guardians also come with them to the principal, who is Malgaras. Again, under these are others, as messengers and doorkeepers, without a fixed number, who often assemble mingled with them. We do not possess the names of all these spirits. But those which it is necessary for the operator to know we shall set forth in each chapter. And note that all these spirits are, each with his principal emperor, in the quarter of the world assigned to him, as is clear in the table.
Book One. Chapter II. Whose prince is called Padiel. Subsolanus, having under him 10,000 daytime ministers, 200,000 nighttime ones, and many other subservitors, whose number is uncertain.

Since, as we said in the preceding chapter, Pamersiel with his aforesaid spirits is implacable and unfaithful, and does not obey indiscriminately all who desire to work in this art, but scarcely even the most experienced in it, we wish in this present chapter to make the art safer, and to demonstrate the manner of working in it through better spirits, who are benevolent, prompt, and cheerful in obeying the one who calls; who, when called in the proper manner and at the proper time, come without delay, and faithfully carry out without any deceit whatever what has been entrusted to them. Now the first principal emperor and presiding spirit of this operation is called Padiel, by the name Subsolanus, in an orbicular mansion, which is the first mansion after the east. He has under him ten thousand who preside over the day and over all daytime operations of this art; they command and bring out the nocturnal spirits lurking in darkness, who number two hundred thousand. All flee light and day, except one who is a messenger to the presiding spirits. All are good and benevolent, and they do not harm the operator unless he is malicious, or less skilled in the art. It is not necessary to call them all together, but a few suffice, and sometimes one can satisfy the operator, whether the operation is nocturnal or diurnal. For since they are
3 Of the Steganography

Let them be kindly disposed, quiet, and calm; they are more often solitary wanderers than noisy in a crowd. Therefore, when you wish to operate through them, and through them to make known the secret of your mind to someone, however absent he may be, do this. Write on paper previously prepared in the proper manner, as you know, whatever account you wish, and in whatever language, since it makes no difference: for he will perceive your mind not from the paper, but from the Spirits. While writing it, turn toward the east; when it is completed, say this conjuration: Padiel aporsy mesarpon omeuas peludyn malpreaxo. Condusen, vlearo thersephi bayl merphon, paroys gebuly mailthomyon ilthear tamarson acrimyon peatha Casmy Chertiel, medony reabdo, lasonti iaciel mal arti bulomeon abry pathulmon theoma parhormyn. When you have completed these words, you will see two, or at least one, of the Spirits very peacefully present and ready to obey your will. And to him you will entrust your secret, and he will faithfully carry it to the place you have commanded.

But when the letters come by messenger to the one to whom they are sent, if he is alone, well; if he is with others, let him withdraw apart if he can, or, if he cannot, let him turn toward the east and say this conjuration in silence: Padiel ariel vanerhon chio thatson phymarto merphon amprisco ledabarym, elsophroy mesarpon ameorsy, paneryn atle pachumgk thearan vtrul vt solubito beslonty las gomadyn triamy mefarnothy. When these words have been duly spoken, immediately the Spirit sent will appear, to reveal it without deceit and without any danger. No one malicious and wicked will easily be able to operate in this art; but the better and purer anyone is, the more willingly and with greater cheerfulness the Spirits obey him. And the more each person conceals this knowledge, the more easily he will operate. And note that this Padiel with his Spirits is appointed to announce secret advisories for the correction of evildoers, imprisonment, and punishment, as we have shown in the example set below.
INTEN-
FIRST BOOK.
THE SECRET OF THE INTENTION, WHICH [unclear] is entrusted not to letters, but to spirits of the second dwelling.
[unclear]

Someone has been denounced to the prince, against whom some crime of lèse-majesté, or any other crime, is alleged. He wishes him to be punished by his official, from whom he is far separated. But he does not wish to write this very thing to him, lest, if the letters are disclosed by any chance, the accused man be warned and flee, or resist after joining to himself the forces of his friends, or contrive some hostile act against the prince or the laws of the country. He writes this or any other narrative whatever to his prefect, one which he need not fear being read by everyone; but the secret he entrusts to a spirit, in the manner we have described above, which will faithfully tell his secret to the man to whom it is sent, who has first been instructed in this art.

Sincere charity. I send you a prayer, for the devotion of penitents, rather beautifully composed and brief, which the whole goodwill of my mind toward you did not wish to possess alone; and it is as follows. Deliver us, Jesus Christ, eternal Savior of all good things, and forgive the offenses of sinners, and hear our groans, calming the storms of vices and renewing the oldness of conscience; lead us back to eternal paradise. Good Jesus, forgive us our sins as we beseech you, since we have grievously offended and have often fallen back. Sweetest Savior, heal our weaknesses, we pray. Be kind to those who pray to you, most dutiful Jesus, and hear us, your servants, as we supplicate you. We are human beings, wretchedly entangled in continual miseries and sunk in the greatest storms. Rescue us, most victorious comforter of the afflicted, since our life, continually buried in frailty, is corrupted. Have mercy at last, most merciful Jesus, Savior; look upon the humility of those who love you, and do not permit us, exiles, to be drowned in the mire and foulness of vices, in the love of the world. Until now we have lain sluggish, and, bound by vices, we have made little account of our salvation and have been scarcely mindful of the coming judgment. Most kind Creator, be propitious to your servants, and save those weeping ones whom the most wretched vanity of the world has deceived. Alas, we have all neglected the way of Truth; but deliver us, fixed in the mire and exiles as we are, since you are our Savior, Jesus, who despise no one. You are the unfailing joy and everlasting happiness of the saints, our hope, the glory of Christians, the light of angels, the rewarder of undefeated martyrs, the crown of virgins, the honor of widows. Good Jesus, hear us, humble [unclear].

The First Book. Chapter III. Whose prince [is] Camuel, having under him 10 spirits presiding over the daytime operations and 10 likewise over the nocturnal, with as many under-servants, whose office is to announce the coming of the one who sends.

The first and supreme of all the spirits of the third mansion, toward the south-east, is called Camuel, very benevolent and prompt to send his substitutes to him who operates in this science according to the due form. He has indeed few ministers, but all good, willing, and faithful—namely ten who preside over the day and as many who preside over the night—who are always sent in pairs to the operator from either order; since those who preside over the day neither flee the darkness, nor those who preside over the night the light. Always, where necessity demands, in every commission of the operator the one is helped by the other; and when they appear visibly, then one is seen in a beautiful habit of mixed color, and the other is wont to stand by in the form of a bright splendor. Often, however, they appear by a sensible effect only, and are not seen, except when it has so pleased the operator. This Camuel, with his ministers and under-servants, has the authority and power of announcing to an absent friend the state, will, condition, way, journeys, coming, and departure of the sender, whenever he himself who operates in this art shall wish. When, therefore, you wish, and operate according to your will, through the angels of this mansion, it behooves you to know first of all who are the ten angels of Camuel who preside over the day, and how many substitutes each of them has, and likewise so of the nocturnal [ones]; which, that you may know perfectly, you will consider the present table.

[Table of angel-names with their numbers of substitutes: Orpeniel 10, Citgara 100, Daniel 10, Dobiel 100, Azimo 10; Camuel 100, Pariel 10, Omyel 10, Nodar 10, Tediel 0; Budiel 10, Cariel 10, Asiniel 100, Phaniel 10, Moriel 0; Elcar 10, Neriel 10, Calym 100, Meras 100, Tugaros 0. — It seemed rather that "Noctar" should be read.]
Here you have in the table the 10 angels of Camuel who preside over the day, with their substitutes in number, and as many who preside over the night, with their [own]…
12, of the Steganography

with their own subordinates as well. The last, however, as you see, have no substitute, since 0, as you know, signifies absolutely nothing in number. Therefore, when you wish to work through these angels, prepare your paper, as is customary; and, turned toward the Eurus, write whatever narrative you wish, in whatever language you wish, which need not be concealed. When it has been completed, read the following conjuration silently: Camuel aperoys, melym meuomanial, casmoyn cralty busaco aeli lumar photirion theor besamys, aneal Cabelonyr thiamo vesonthy. When this conjuration has been completed in silence, give your commission to the spirits who are present, as you know; send them forth, doing everything in silence and without commotion, if it can be done. Afterwards give the letters, to be carried through, to whatever messenger you wish, open, so that he may go freely, because the spirits will not neglect their duty, whether the messenger comes quickly or late; of this let there be no doubt for you, for they are faithful. But you must know which spirit from those named above you wish to send, so that in the conjuration you express his name immediately after the principal one; this applies in all operations in which the names of the angels to be sent are set down in the chapter itself. But now let us set down an example of what we have said concerning those things that pertain to the office of Camuel and of his subject spirits.
Roth.

Let This Be The Most Secret Intention Of My Mind, which I wish an absent person to know through the aforesaid spirits. When I am situated at Rome, I understand from the most secret counsel of the supreme pontiff that he wishes to transfer the Roman Empire itself to the Franks. I desire to dare [unclear] the princes of Germany: by messengers I cannot, since I do not trust them; by letters I cannot, because in all the cities of Italy there are men appointed at the gates who examine passers-by most exactly. Therefore I write one devout prayer, which I send open by a messenger, along with other familiar letters closed, to the same princes. Let us imagine the secret of your mind. You have a beloved woman, in whose love you are held, and she no less; but you cannot approach or speak to her because of the watch kept by her people. At last you have found a plan by which you can possess her, but it is necessary first to advise her of it. You cannot do so yourself; you do not dare by letters, lest they come into the hands of others; nor do you decide that the matter should be entrusted to messengers or old women, lest afterward they make you known. Therefore, conceal by art for a time the matter which you trust cannot be made openly. You call the invisible ministers of the art, write letters suspected in nothing, and send them to your beloved even through those same guardians; they praise the writing and give it to your beloved to read. Recognizing the sign, she calls the hidden messenger, hears the plan, sends back her consent; you approach, enter, obtain possession.

By living justly we shall attain happiness; for only the humble are to be exalted, only the rash to be condemned. If you seek happiness, hold fast eternal justice; you will obtain the highest glory. Be a most fervent zealot for truth; do not love falsehood, corrupting honesty and dissolving the moderation of the soul. Flee the vanity of the world, since it is very brief. Be a lover of Justice, supplanting no one unjustly. Cultivate the virtues, flee vices; justice [unclear] freedom; beware all insolence; always be humble. Love the Savior of our souls: he who loves him will by no means die unhappily. Despise glory that passes suddenly away; love the blessedness of the saints, not to be corrupted eternally. Carefully flee the snares of our ancient enemy, whom the humility of devotion, never to be interrupted, will conquer. Be watchful, so that you are not overcome by the heat of the flesh; defend manfully the paths of justice, and you know that the guilty man of rectitude is subject to everlasting evils. Every proud man is hateful to God: dying, he will be tortured without interruption and will never be consoled. What, finally, will the proud expect except lamentation? Therefore woe to you who are exalted, worthy of eternal punishment and reserved for everlasting darkness and horrors. O most pernicious vanity of vanities. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, wrote this on the Ides of March, 1500.

The highest nobility and the highest virtue of the human race is to love God purely, to seek his glory, and to adore him with uprightness of mind. For the humility of a pure heart shall reign in heaven; patience shall exalt the mind alone of a bare man. He who fears God and is most diligent shall be established in true nobility. Love God, despise the world, flee the age of iniquity, love religion, brotherly charity, the bond of peace, and the unity of those who live rightly. Christ admonishes in the Gospel that we ought not to be anxious about superfluous human cares. “Having,” says the holy Apostle, “only what is necessary, let us be content.” Let us therefore have the love of God and zeal for justice, since truly solid riches are purity of soul, simplicity of heart, disregard of earthly honor, the cleansing of beauty, and the instruction of holy morals. Let us be intent upon good works, lest vices overwhelm us; let us live innocent in all uprightness, as though we were to die tomorrow. Let us love God with a most pure heart, carefully keeping [unclear] his with humility; let us mourn for sins, at all times beseeching the most pious Savior that he may forgive us our vices and pour into us his love and humility of heart. Let us defer the desires of this world and vain and false honors, diligently thinking upon our death. To live virtuously, to love one’s neighbor, to do injury to no one, to fear God, to give alms, to feed the hungry, to defend the good, to rebuke the vices of the depraved, to persist in prayers, to despise the glory of the world, and to devote oneself to readings: these are the treasures of Christians. For the vain glory of the world is about to fall suddenly, and riches too are false, which, when we shortly breathe our last, we shall leave behind unwillingly. Justice alone is our happiness. In our humility there is glorying, and the possession of riches that will remain with us for all time: the memory of death, fear of judgment, and recollection of our sins.

The counsel of a prince is great and most secret, concerning very great and difficult matters. He wishes some other prince, a friend, to know it, because he has cause; but he fears that it may come into public, with the greatest danger to himself and his people; if, however, it is entrusted to a messenger, he fears lest he betray it, or to letters, lest they be read by someone. Therefore he calls a spirit, who will not reveal the secret; he entrusts it, accomplishes it, and is secure.
He sends letters in no respect suspect, nor fearing public exposure in any respect. Roth.

Jesus Christ, unfailing light, eternal blessedness of all the saints, creator and ruler of the universe, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and weeping, ask your mercy. Grant us the strength to overcome the temptations of the devil, so that, with present evils avoided, we may obtain rest. O sweetest Savior Jesus, forgive the sins of us, the servants who pray, since we desire to serve you with all our strength. Make us always have in ourselves the fervor of your love, adorned with good works. Give us the true operations of virtues, observance of justice, and inseparable love of uprightness; make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with your love, we may love nothing earthly, and esteem nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, Jesus Christ, teach us to imitate your doctrine. We are, alas, entangled in many vices, bare of good works. Save us, Jesus Christ, lest we perish. O highest truth, make us alive, refuge of souls, refresh-

[unclear]: be to us a tower of strength. For you are our life-giver, you are the salvation of souls, and the sweetest renewer of the mind. You are the ineffable joy of the angels, and the most wholesome rest of faithful spirits. You are the blessedness of the saints who love you. You are the inextinguishable light of the citizens above. You, life-giver of the dead, look upon our frailty. Sweetest Jesus Christ, help us, your frail servants, so that, walking without stumbling along the way of truth, we may attain eternal rest. O most merciful Lord Jesus, soften the labors of our exile. And when the end of this life shall begin to draw near, may you then deign mercifully to come to our aid, so that before the face of your power the adversary may fall in terror, and the devils, the inciters of all evils, the princes of eternal death and our most savage persecutors, may flee far away. We beseech you by the power of your most noble death, sweetest Jesus: do not despise us, your useless servants, on the day of our departure, whom you willed to redeem by your blood. Wash away our transgressions, so that we may deserve to enter the joys of the heavenly fatherland, while the angels await us. Amen.

Health and affection. My most beloved and most singular friend, the bearer of the present letter, a native of Roermond, very beneficent and [unclear] toward our friends, whom I ask you to receive kindly, will explain his need to you. Most Illustrious Prince, I inform Your Grace that Conrad Hummel, beneficed at the altar of St. John the Evangelist, died last night. But lest Your Grace, without deliberation, grant the said altar either to one of the unskilled or unworthy, of whom I think a great number will be present, as is usually the case, expecting the said altar, instead of reserving it for a more useful man, I beg that, although I am far too unworthy for my prayers to seem to obtain any favor in the sight of so great and noble a prince, Your Grace may deign worthily to grant the aforesaid altar to the bearer of the present letters, rejecting the less worthy. I have known him to be worthy of the best benefices, since I know him to be adorned with beauty of character, learned in every way in knowledge and letters, modest, continent, temperate, and one whose love of religion will be pleasing to Your Grace. I send you an oration that I composed at the wedding of a certain friend of mine. God, creator of all things, redeemer of the human race, and savior of all, lest the human race should perish, also instituted the sacrament of marriage; for we read that he joined Eve as wife to the first man and said: INCREASE AND MULTIPLY, instituting the law for preserving humanity. Afterwards God incarnate deigned to sanctify marriages by a miracle. I shall praise those who serve God well by keeping the marital [unclear]; although I am not married, I shall nevertheless rightly praise marriages.

Indeed, if marriage were taken away, the whole human race would fail and collapse. For by the use of marriages the human race exists, although ruinous, weak, and corruptible; yet without marriages it would not endure. But act in such a way that the fruitfulness of your marriages is adorned with morals and conduct, holy, and placing a stumbling-block before no one. First of all love God, continually applying yourselves to works of mercy with justice; flee impiety, cultivate rectitude, love the good, always speak praises to God, assist the poor with alms, obey the commandments of God. Do not forsake truth; honor the ministers of God; pay tithes to the churches; receive pilgrims as guests; free the innocent; feed the hungry; obey your superiors; honorably love your neighbors, inflicting injury on absolutely no one. Cultivate the Christian religion most devoutly; abhor the vain, harmful, and superstitious customs of the gentiles. Keep the teachings of the Gospels and live according to the precepts of God. Flee the pleasures of the flesh, and show yourselves honorable and good; anxiously guard purity of mind

keeping [it], do not defile [it]. Remember, I beseech you, what Christ our Lord cried out in the holy Gospel: Blessed are the pure in heart, that is, those who preserve purity of soul in a muddy body for God’s sake. Let purity of heart not be without continual and most humble prayers, since prayer purifies the mind, cools those who are burning, and drives far away the temptations of the devil. Hence the most holy Apostle Paul teaches you to persist in diligent and devout prayers, so that you may overcome harmful temptations. We join you in marriage, so that you may build up your lineage, propagated by decree of law, not so that you ought to overflow with harmful pleasures. For the pleasures of the flesh kill the soul and corrupt the noblest dignity of human substance [for] things to come. Therefore, mindful of these things, know that you are wayfarers who will return to the fatherland to which you have been called back. The present life is very brief, and the delight of the world comes most swiftly to an end. Therefore live in marriage in such a way that after death you may come to the kingdom of heaven with [exultation?]. Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, of the order of God’s father Benedict, issued [this] on the day before the Ides of March, in the year of the nativity of the Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

The ancients define Justice and Philosophy as the greatest ornament of nobility, and Impiety and Ignorance as its disgrace. For what is more beautiful than to adorn a noble family, which serves as a soldier, with letters and virtues? We find that very many others, and numerous very noble men serving as soldiers, did this by night and by day, so that they might subdue barbarians by arms, and by uprightness instruct their people and with letters. By their example, [Buma vv?], most learned, [unclear] the letters of humanity and the good arts [unclear], acknowledged, adorned with arms and letters. The wisest princes of old were accustomed not to shut up their wealth in their treasuries, but rather to devote it to literary use, judging the study of wisdom to be the most honorable support for those tending toward happiness, by which the blessedness of eternal retribution is acquired. Indeed, knowledge of the Scriptures makes princes venerable to all, and especially to be feared. Ignorance of the Scriptures, called the burial of a living man, has been accustomed to bring shame and horrible calamity upon noble princes. A man without letters is a two-footed ass, to be buried alive, or rather already buried. It is especially necessary that nobles who govern the commonwealth be wise and notable for knowledge of letters; their ignorance brings in tyranny. Love of letters also commends the renowned deeds of princes and nobles to perpetuity. For we see that ancient philosophers obtained the memory of rule, and attained immortality of name, everlasting among all men more by letters than by arms. For letters made the glorious, excellent, and wise ancient tyrants and princes more so than arms did, and endowed the memory and titles of their praises with immortality. Add that, for Christians, the study of letters provides the highest and most honorable aid for flying to Heaven. For from the Scriptures we begin to contemplate the flashing and honorable majesty of divine illuminations, to us

Of these, some are not useless to us for Steganography, because they do not require the observance of places, but can be summoned by conjuration in every place. The first of these is called Geradiel; he does not have any [count?] or prince under him, but only many servants, almost innumerable, whom he takes with him for service according to the ranks that they have among themselves, according to the twenty-four hours of day and night. Their general office is to announce secretly whatever things you wish, to whatever quarter.

CHAPTER XXIV.
Whose prince is called Pyrichiel, having under him many leaders, princes, companions, and servants, whose number is uncertain.

Pyrichiel, a certain supreme prince of spirits, seems to us to have to be wholly rejected from our art, because he is said to be quite benevolent. He does not have under him leaders or princes in the manner of the rest, but only companions and subordinate servants, whose number is uncertain. There are those who say that he has leaders and princes under him; they seem to us not to understand his property and custom well enough, since they have imagined companions and servants as leaders. The name of Pyrichiel derives its designation from fire, because he is frequently accustomed to be occupied around fire.

Let us amend our life, humbling ourselves before the highest maker of the universe. Humility obtains Heaven; it annihilates the harmful temptations of demons; it restrains the pernicious swelling of the mind, and powerfully exterminates all fires of vices. …[the secrets] of wisdom, nor does nature help, when they have not been able to understand this most secret art of our invention—[this] is not to be imputed to us, but rather they will understand it is to be ascribed to their own sloth, laziness, and malice: namely those who, having their wit immersed in the pleasures of the flesh and worldly cares, cannot with diligence be at leisure to survey these things; or who, deeming themselves already wise or most learned, despise our compositions as unworthy of their reading. There will be also some so accustomed to rest in old and alien traditions that they deem whatever they have not learned in them either impossible or superstitious. Nothing is more inept for the knowledge of this profound art than these, who either will not or cannot contemplate its loftiest [matters]. But those who are both apt and willing to study in this art (if any there shall be)—that they may be able to make progress—we have determined to admonish in a few [words] at the end of this book. First of all they are to be admonished that they always keep the art itself hidden, lest it penetrate the hand and notice of the wicked, who would do many and execrable crimes through it. For although the art itself is truly good in itself, yet its practice would conduce no less to evil through the impious than to good through the good. Let the secret therefore remain among the good, which, published among the wicked, would do harm. Nor, however, ought the good to despise this knowledge because it profits the wicked unto evil; just as he who lays a man low does not spurn the sword. Then the studious of this art are to be admonished not to presume to proceed to operating in it, unless first they have been perfectly instructed in all [things] which are required for the practical science. For it does not escape me to how great dangers they subject the matter who, less skilled, have at any time attempted to operate something in it. Likewise, whoever, well instructed in this science, shall wish to operate through it, let him remember to observe diligently (according to those [things] which we have said, as much in the circle as in the individual tables and chapters) the difference, the places, names, orders, and offices of the supreme Spirits, their dukes also, and how many counts there are in number; which order let him obser[ve]…

observe, and who are placed over the substitutes, so that he may know how to express these things in the conjuration. For unless the practitioner of the art has carefully observed all these things, he will not be able to make progress, nor to arrive at the effect of his intention. Again, let him attend carefully when each spirit is to be called for which duties or secrets, and in what quarter of the world he dwells, lest he err either in the places or in the [names?] of the several ones whom he wishes to call.

Likewise, let everyone who is to operate in this science be advised to attend most diligently to pronouncing the words of the conjurations properly, for in them lies the great force of our operation; since, when an error is committed in the conjurations, the spirits called, or to be called, not only do not obey, but even wholly resist. Consequently, let him also be forewarned not to call one for another, but each one in his own order, time, and office, just as has been sufficiently stated by us in nearly all the chapters of this book. For if, either through error or through any other negligence, he calls one for another, he will make no progress in his operation, but will bring danger upon himself.

Likewise, in the conjurations the spirit who is called should be expressed by name together with his substitutes; the cause of the calling should first be fixed in the intention; nor should the act of operation be performed in light, profane matters, which one person can otherwise communicate safely to another without danger, whether by letters or by messengers. For this art is to be used only for announcing great and difficult matters which, if made public, would bring loss or danger upon the operator. Likewise, it is necessary for everyone operating in this art to know the natures of the spirits: which are good, which evil, which ready and well-disposed to obedience, which harsh and rebellious. Again, which preside over nocturnal operations, and which over diurnal ones; because unless he has known the natures of the spirits before he begins to operate, he will make progress with the greatest difficulty and will easily be turned to stupor. Likewise, when the spirits called appear visibly before the operator, after the secret word has been sent ahead, let him entrust the secret of his mind to the duke or count in appropriate words, under silence; for there is no need to speak to the spirit in a raised voice, but let him use a low one.

Care must also be taken with the greatest diligence, both by the operator and by the recipient, that they do not perform anything pertaining to Steganography in the presence of other men ignorant of this art, when they can have access to a secret place. But if they cannot be alone, and it happens that they are compelled to operate among others, let them act so secretly, so prudently, and with such industry that none of those sitting around understands anything about the presence of the spirits. For all the spirits assigned to the ministry of this art are of such a nature and condition that they utterly detest and flee the tumult of men, and hate a public gathering. Likewise, the operator must also take care not to direct any spirit anywhere without letters, or at least without the character of his emperor; for when he does not see that very character impressed, he utterly refuses to obey the one calling him and to carry the secret to anyone. We send letters for a twofold reason, although we could announce the secret without letters through the spirit alone: namely, so that we may preserve from suspicion the men carrying the character, and so that, by that very character, we may constrain the spirit bound to obey the friend.

Preface.

In the preceding book, relying on the help of the highest God, we arranged in order, not without great labor, the thirty-one supreme spirits, emperors of our art, together with their dukes, counts, and servants necessary for us in operation. Although their ministries are abundantly sufficient for every operator for the announcement of all secrets, however secret, still, lest we seem to omit anything that can conduce to the perfection of this art, we have resolved to join a second book to the first. Since, moreover, by the tradition of certain wise men, individual spirits have been assigned to the individual hours of day and night for various operations and diverse and wondrous effects, it has pleased us to imitate only their order, not their superstition, so that, without injury to the Christian name, we may take from them what conduces to our purpose; but the rest, as being full of magical arts and contrary to our faith,

[unclear] let us pass through by laying low [unclear]. Therefore, taking up, for each single hour both of day and of night, the principal spirits appointed by the secret of Solomon, surnamed Hermes, in his volume On Magic, as the supreme emperors of the art, together with the other officials necessary to us for the operation proposed, we shall proceed; and we shall give both method and instruction to all students in this art, by which at any hour they may disclose the secret and hidden conception of their minds to friends with safer counsel. For each prince presides like a watchman over his spirits, dukes, counts, and servants; at his command, when summoned by us with a lawful song, they come; they carry the entrusted secrets, and show themselves obedient and ready for us in all things. But since I am going to mention spirits again, I think I must preface once more: nothing in this art of ours is held to be frivolous; nothing contrary to evangelical tradition or the Catholic faith; nothing at all superstitious is handed down. For everything that we have said in the preceding volume, or shall say in those that follow, is supported by natural, lawful, and honorable principles; and the mystery veiled only by foreign institutions, and words wrapped in the names of spirits, require a learned reader. For we use the service of a spirit to veil a secret which, if published, would harm the reprobate. And lest anyone fail through error in the reckoning of the hours, let him know that we have accepted the hours of the planets both by day and by night.

The emperor-spirit of the first hour of the day, which takes its beginning at sunrise, is called Samael. He has under his command many dukes, counts, and subordinate servants; when summoned by the operator in this hour only, in Steganography, they come. They carry the secret that is entrusted to them, but they utterly refuse to come outside the hour. And note that Samael's first dukes, the princes, are rarely sent by him into the service of this science, since they hold office in stirring up men's magical nocturnal illusions. But the counts, with their attendants, have been specially appointed to the service of this art; into this they are also more often sent without the presence of the dukes. Since they are from the highest order among spirits, they are accustomed to show themselves somewhat proud and rebellious to those who summon them, nor do they easily obey anyone, unless he is most skilled in the art of Steganography, without labor and danger. For they are impudent, very ready for illusions and mockeries of men, and they especially deride and jeer at those whom they find to be less skilled in the art of Steganography. But those whom they consider bold, steadfast, and experienced in that art, they respect and fear, and they always obey their commands most promptly, with trembling reverence. And so now we shall report the names of those counts who are necessary to us in the operations of Steganography in this hour.

Those matters which you proposed to me to be resolved, with Christ’s help, I have resolved. Whether well, you who proposed them shall pronounce judgment. I shall briefly report to you an astonishing event that took place. A certain brother recently reported to me, as did one friend, not the least, that a young man had been raised from the dead at the invocation of Christ, reporting wondrous and dreadful things among the lower regions, narrating the torments of wicked Christians, namely of those who by acting perversely crucified Christ; that they were especially guilty of this, that, forgetful of the benefit of most gracious redemption, they always showed themselves ungrateful to Christ; and that those suffer dreadful things who, known to be ungrateful for his benefits by not living well, and blinded by sin, neglected future joys while following the pleasures of the world. They, bitten by the negligence they had committed, cried out most bitterly: Deservedly we endure these things, we who were always ungrateful to the redeemer of the human race: Christians in name, heathens in deed. Why did we despise the time granted to us? The raised young man reported to us many deep things, which I am utterly unable to write, especially being weighed down by serious business. In which we shall teach the general method and form of approaching this art of Steganography, and of operating in it without danger, with the greatest usefulness.

Whoever desires to approach the knowledge of this hidden art of ours; whoever wishes to work wonders through it, and things useful to many amid dangers: first of all he must be adorned with virtues, and be of clean conscience and good will toward God, toward himself, and toward his neighbor, so that he is not inclined to harm anyone, nor seeks dealings of baseness. Then it is necessary that he be somewhat imbued with the good arts of letters, and especially with the science of the stars, so that he may know the general motions, courses, wanderings, changes, orders, natures, positions, risings, settings, and effects of the stars, signs, and planets; because without competent knowledge of these no one can have access to the depths of this art. Consequently it is necessary that he have a teacher perfect and experienced in the art, because we believe it possible to come to this science without a teacher only for a few, and for those most learned in many things, and especially skilled in magical matters. These are the seven angels, according to the tradition of the ancient sages, each of whom guides the world for three hundred fifty-four years and four months in his order. Orifiel is the angel of Saturn, who from the beginning of creation governed the world for 354 years and 4 months. Afterwards Venus, then Jupiter, after him Mercury, and then Mars, afterwards the Moon, afterwards the Sun. Each is described as having held dominion over the world for 354 years and 4 months, with his angel written in the table common to him. And so the sages report that at the time of the flood Samael, the angel of Mars, served the authority of rule; Gabriel, however, the angel of the Moon, at the time of the confusion of tongues; Michael, the angel of the Sun, at the time of Israel's departure from Egypt. And indeed, if anyone gives credence to the aforesaid assertion, he will easily be able by himself, from the origin of the world down to his own age, to calculate the changes of times and the governance of the angels in the order prescribed. But we, pursuing those things that serve our purpose, do not doubt that under the seven aforesaid angels of the planets there are subject twenty-one other spirits, that is, three to each one, according to the instruction of this art of ours; through them we accomplish the effect of our intention. We shall observe the customary order of the planets, beginning from Saturn, the highest of all, down to the Moon, first writing down the operation of each principal angel, and then of those serving under them, and joining the chapters together in order.

Chapter I
On Orifiel, the first and supreme angel of Saturn, and on the operations that are performed through him.

Saturn, the highest and supreme of all the planets, slow in motion and by nature, cold because remote, difficult, heavy, from the point of its beginning 650 years up to the point of its first station, remaining in each sign for 30 months, is moved by its natural proper motion 626. Its first and supreme angel is called, according to the opinion of the ancients, Orifiel, who has under him three other principal spirits, namely Sadael, Poniel, and Morisiel, of whom we shall speak in their proper place and order.

Through this Orifiel, the great angel of Saturn, many different operations are performed in steganography. Through him we can make the secret of our mind known to a friend who knows the art, wherever he may be: by letters, if one wishes, or even without letters, and do many other marvelous things, which no one else understands who is unskilled in this science of ours. Therefore, anyone wishing to perform anything through this angel in steganography, especially on the day of Saturn, in these matters, business, and causes that pertain to Saturn, must first know its various and diverse motions. And first the various motion: pure, proper, mixed, direct, retrograde, and confused. And in all these he must know not only the general rules handed down by the astronomers, because although they are very useful for this science of ours, nevertheless they do not wholly suffice, but also the particular rules.

Therefore, once the tables and rules concerning the motions of the planets have been laid down as a foundation, which anyone working in this art must know completely, we have added special rules and tables of punctual motions throughout the individual chapters of this work; without observing them no one will be able to operate in this art. And note that the day of each planet is divided into four equal parts, of which the principal angel of that planet obtains the first, that is, three unequal hours; and his substitutes in order take the remaining three parts. For example: on the day of Saturn, Orifiel, its first angel, possesses the three unequal hours from sunrise, which are called the hours of the planets; Sadael, his first angel, possesses the second three; Pomiel, the second, holds the third; and Morisiel, the third angel of Orifiel, holds the last three hours. In the first three hours of the day both of Saturn and of the other stars, in matters appropriated to Saturn, one must operate through Orifiel; in the second, through Sadael; in the third, through Pomiel; and in the last three, through Morisiel. And all operations, according to the motion of Saturn, receive either a prosperous effect or a weak one. But now let us set down the punctual table.

While you are making it, say: Let this image of great Orifiel be full, perfect, and fit to announce the secret of my mind to N., son of N., my friend, securely, faithfully, and completely. Amen. Write on the forehead your own name with ink tempered with oil of roses, and on the breast the name of your absent friend, saying: This is the image of N., son of N., to whom through Orifiel, angel of Saturn, the conception of my mind is announced. Hear, Orifiel, prince of the star of Saturn, and by the powers of almighty God I adjure you, listen: I command and order you, by the power of this image of yours, that you announce to N., son of N., this intention of mine (let the intention be explained) as quickly as possible, securely, secretly, and faithfully, omitting nothing of those things which I want him to know, and which I have entrusted to you. Then wrap those images, thus fastened together, in a cloth washed with water of white [wine?], and put them in a movable vessel, which the wise call Indix pharnat alronda; cover it carefully above with shaved leather, and put it in the entrance of some closed dwelling, wherever you wish, for the space of 24 hours; and without any hesitation your desire will be perfectly fulfilled within those 24 hours. And your absent friend will know your intention in every form most perfectly, just as you spoke it over the image, however long it may have been; and whatever you wish him to know from you, he will know within those 24 hours perfectly and most secretly, so that no man will ever be able to perceive or know this for all eternity without your will or that of your friend. And it is a great secret, which none of the wise before us dared to commit to writing. But that friend of yours, if he wishes you to know anything from his affairs, can make you more certain through the same spirit within the same space of 24 hours, provided he is well perfected in this art. But you, when 24 hours have elapsed, take the images from the place in which they were put, and put them away, because at every time of Orifiel you can operate through them not only for that friend of yours, but for any others whatsoever, merely changing the name of that friend into the name of the person whom you wish to know something. Preface of Johannes Trithemius

It is the opinion of the wise that the ancient philosophers of art and nature, who had discovered secrets, concealed them by various methods and figures, so that they might not come to the knowledge of wicked men. The more learned among the Jews also confirm that Moses, the most famous leader of the Israelite people, in his description of the creation of heaven and earth, disclosed ineffable mysteries of secrets in simple words. Saint Jerome, most learned among our own, says that in the Apocalypse almost as many mysteries lie hidden as there are words. Moreover, the wise men of the Greeks, of no small esteem among their own people, who devoted their effort to writing fables, with most prudent reasoning handed down one thing to the unlearned and another to the wise in the course of a single narration. I cannot but admire these most zealous lovers of wisdom, and I do not fail to read them with whatever industry I can, so that, while I consider that they labored by lamplight more greatly than other men, I may, as best I can, fill the empty belly of my memory with certain crumbs, as it were, of knowledge falling from the table of the rich philosophers.

Nor, as I think, has this opinion altogether deceived me, since by the continual labor of reading I have learned many things that I did not know, and in various ways I have reserved an approach for my thoughts toward investigating greater secrets of things. Although, indeed, I am not of such great learning or industry that I would dare profess that I have grasped that secret method of the ancient sages which they used in concealing the majesty of philosophy, nevertheless I have devised certain methods, not to be despised, as it seems to me, of writing altogether secretly and without any suspicion, and of concealing whatever you wish. At the urging of the most serene prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince-Elector of the Roman Empire, the wisest patron of philosophers, than whom no one seemed to me more worthy, I committed these methods to writing and gathered them into the following volume, not without enormous labor.

But lest this great secret come to the ears of the unlearned or of wicked men, whoever you may be as reader, I warn, ask, and adjure you by the ineffable name of God, JEHOVAH, and by the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, that you disclose this science of writing to no one unworthy, immodest, carnal, or maliciously old, since through it many things could be done among men: adulteries, fornications, conspiracies, murders, and betrayals, if, which may it not happen, it were made known. For just as a good and honorable man, as often as it is necessary, can safely and without any suspicion from anyone make known and express the secret of his will to another person who knows the art, for private or common advantage, so a perverse man, immodest and blinded by carnal love, can signify to a consenting person of his desire, however shamelessly, foully, and lustfully, his evil desire, by honorable, modest, and holy words, determining the place, time, and manner of meeting, as broadly as he can, without any suspicion. Nor will there henceforth be any security among married people, while a woman can very easily understand the evil will of her lover from the best writings, with her husband looking on and praising the most holy words, without any suspicion of evil; and whatever you wish your mistress to know, however ignorant she may be of Latin words, she can send back in reply, with her husband marveling and, as is possible, carrying the message. Indeed, if this science were to come to the knowledge of the commonwealth, the whole order would be disturbed, public trust would perish, letters, documents, all writings, and the very conversations of men would be turned into the gravest suspicion. No one now by letters, however

whenever thereafter no one would believe good, holy, and honorable men; no one would put trust in letters, however holy and chaste their words might be; it would always be thought that deceit, fraud, and evil deception lay hidden in the mouth, and men would become fearful about everything, no less suspicious of mutual conversations than of any letters whatever. But let someone object to me, saying: If you wanted this knowledge of yours to be hidden, why did you wish to commit it to writing? To him I say, if an answer must be given, that I neither ought nor could hide this knowledge from the most excellent prince, by means of which he may, if occasion arises, be able to free his dependants, of whose number I am one, from many dangers. For by means of this knowledge he can make known the conception of his mind to his own people, to whomever he wishes, secretly or openly, securely, without in the least fearing anyone's knowledge to the contrary. But whoever wishes to write anything by this art should diligently observe the methods, signs, and proportions of each thing; if he neglects to consider these, he himself will easily be able to forget what he has written. But now, with the Lord's help, let us proceed to the demonstration.

Precautions to Be Observed

But it must be observed that the aforesaid method, as we have said, is not sufficiently safe in serious matters, since as soon as any suspicion begins to arise about the letters, the secret can easily be detected by a clever person. Therefore the following methods are safer, as is clear. Likewise it must be observed, if by this or other methods you write to someone not sufficiently learned in the Latin language, that he should not divide the words, lest [unclear]. If you wish, you may use two points; I fill each word of your secret so that, when you have made a complete sentence of the outer text, you may make a little stroke thus, or the reverse, as you like. Yet it seems safer that neither points nor little strokes be made; and let the sign of a period, of whatever method, be placed not in the word of the secret, but rarely; place it neither over the first letter nor after the last, just as I did above in the hidden tenor: Dear fa[unclear]ithful one, etc.

Extension of This First Method

The first method itself of writing secretly, like nearly all the others, can be varied with manifold diversity, so that a person who perfectly understands the aforesaid order of concealing may still be able to perceive only with difficulty other methods to be inferred from it. For anyone can vary this method, together with the others, for his own book: namely, so that the first line is conscious of the secret, the second not; or, if it is of such size, that one is not; and so consequently the concealer of secrets, as he wishes, is alternated in alternate lines, either whole or half, by descending from the beginning of his letters to the end, or by ascending from the end to the beginning. I add also that from either side, descending and ascending [unclear] another beside the sense of his hidden [unclear] can be varied by powers so many and so diverse that, in explaining them, there is need of an Oedipus. But my present purpose is to show first the simple methods of writing, and to give to those who are worthy and suitable to know many things an occasion by which they may be able elegantly to devise the greatest things from the smallest.
The Second Method, Prudently Varied by Alternate Words, Easy and Very Safe in Every Language

The second method of writing hidden things without suspicion is that the words of the narrative of the openly proposed text be varied by alternate position: namely, so that when the first letter of the first word bears witness to the hidden intention, the first letter of the following word is free from the duty of the secret office. Afterwards the third is not free from the ministry, the fourth remains idle, and so consequently the words, mixed always in alternate turns, serve the secret, while those suited to the public discourse withdraw in prudent order from the signification of hidden things. And this method, easy in every language of the world, contains [unclear] and seems to me sufficiently safe for announcing whatever secrets you wish. Its example is as follows.

The third method is to use alternate words in such a way that the first is always without the meaning of the secret.

The third method of secret writing, as I have said, arises from the preceding one; in it the words serving the secret are varied in alternate turns as above. And this method is very safe and is not easily detected by one ignorant of the art; and we shall set down an example of this kind.

The fifth mode, not very dissimilar to the fourth, proceeds in the customary way with the first null through two signifying words. Seventh Example.

Unfailing light, blessedness of all the saints and creator [unclear], I.C. [unclear] of the universe and ruler, have mercy on us. We, weak, groaning, and thirsting for your mercy, ask you: grant us the strength to overcome the temptations of the Devil, so that, after hard labors for you, we may deserve rest. O sweetest Savior, I pray, look upon your humble servants and useless servants; be merciful to us, since we desire with all our longings to serve you. Make us have the favor of your love always burning within us. Give us the strong bond of brotherly charity. Jesus, almighty King of heaven, make us truly humble and vigorous despisers of worldly things, so that, always burning with love for you, we may love nothing here and regard nothing temporal as pleasant to us. O teacher of humility, most gentle Jesus, teach us to imitate your doctrine; for we are subject to various evils, intent on few goods. Save us, Lord, lest we perish. O supreme truth, give us life; sweet refuge of souls, be to us a tower of strength. For you are our strongest virtue; you are the salvation of my soul and the most healthful refreshment of my mind; you are the ineffable joy of the angels and the rest of all the faithful. You are the holy gladness of those who love you. You are the inextinguishable name of the citizens above. You are the giver of life to the dead and the most merciful sustainer of the frail. You, sweetest Jesus, help us, your frail servants, so that we may deserve to walk along the way of truth on the right path without offense. O most loving Lord Jesus, mitigate my very hard exile; and when the end of this life of mine begins to draw near, deign mercifully to come to our aid then, since [unclear], and fleeing far away all those who intend evils, they will soon be destroyed, since you are our protector. We ask by the virtue of your most noble death, sweetest one: do not despise your servants on the day of our departure, but may Jesus the Lord redeem and wash each of us with your blood, and may all [unclear] of our transgression graciously grant us, as we wait, the heavenly joys of the celestial homeland. Amen.
The hidden tenor of the above.
Dear faithful one, we have understood your business,
[unclear], very quietly, so that we may anticipate the enemy and strike them down.
The eighth method proceeds alternately by three empty words and the same number of significant words.

As the sixth does by two, so namely that any single mystical word of equal syllables completes the meaning of the open narrative in such a way that, when three empty places have been left, the following one begins not from [unclear], but from three significant words. If the word of the secret has unequal syllables, it will receive [unclear] into its company, until the syllables before the period in some way at last become equal.
Eighth example.

O almighty, eternal God, most kindly rewarder of justice, who willed your Son to become a participant in our race, that he might redeem those long placed in most wretched perdition, overflowing with goodness alone, assuming our form incorrupt from the flower of the virginal womb, as the holy Archangel Gabriel made known; which Virgin, destined to conceive by the most blessed Spirit, was to remain a virgin forever, free from crime, more eminent than all men and angels, bore the almighty King, God and man: the most holy and most reverend Virgin Mary, wholly ignorant of male companionship, giving birth without pain, and always remaining such, most high and immaculate. Holy virgin Mother of Jesus Christ, created by the power of God, known everywhere to the humble, filled with love toward other men, existing most worthy of all praise, and always remaining a virgin, [unclear] of the most blessed angels, whom then the Son admits with most generous favor in all things she has asked; and he venerates her as his most reverend mother, more excellent than all creatures, he who has never been accustomed to deny anything to one asking, but at once consents to her most holy will, granting all things, at last through the merits of this advocate of the poor. Therefore, venerating the very renowned merits of the most noble Virgin Mary, Lord Emperor of the universe, we pray that you pour the light of truth into us, wipe away the stains of sins, and truly bestow grace, especially at every time upon those who seek you; remove temptations; grant us, who beseech you, the power of conquering; clothe us with your love, chastity
